title: Weld an L-shaped seam with a TIG torch and filler rod
instruction: Weld the joint between the white and yellow marks with the TIG torch, dabbing the filler rod into the front of the pool to lay one sound bead, then put both tools back on their rests and move both hands away.
context: Manual welding is core daily work for welders, cutters, solderers and brazers (about 420,000 US workers) and, with sheet metal workers (120,000), structural metal fabricators and fitters (52,000) and boilermakers (10,000), for about 600,000 workers in all (BLS, 2025). TIG (GTAW) is the manual process used where the bead must be precise. It takes two hands at once: one carries the torch along the joint at a steady 2-5 mm arc length, and the other dabs filler rod into the front of the pool and withdraws it, so that neither the rod nor the plate ever touches the tungsten, which would contaminate it and stop the weld.
setup: A steel fixture-table top (29 x 27 cm, 12 mm thick, dark grey, a 50 mm hole grid; x 11.5 to 40.5 cm, y -13.5 to 13.5 cm) on the station table. On it, two 6 mm mild-steel plates, held by three blue strap clamps, meet in an L-shaped butt joint with 45 degree bevels 2 mm deep each side (a 4 mm V, dark root line): an inner plate (15 x 11 cm, x 19.5 to 34.5, y -9 to 2 cm) and an L-shaped plate around it (x 14.5 to 34.5, y 2 to 7 cm, plus x 14.5 to 19.5, y -9 to 2 cm). The joint runs 12 cm along -x from the start (31.5, 2) cm to the corner (19.5, 2) cm, then 8 cm along -y to the end (19.5, -6) cm: 200 mm in all. A white paint mark (6 x 30 mm) is beside the start and a yellow one (30 x 6 mm) beside the end. The TIG torch (255 g) lies on two steel rest posts (45 mm tall) on a steel base, its glass-filled nylon grip block (30 x 36 x 26 mm, orange) centred at (20, 21) cm: a 22 mm rubber-covered handle 11 cm long with a 4 cm stub of power cable behind it, a black head 24 mm across with its axis 17.5 degrees from vertical, a pink ceramic cup (14 to 18 mm across, 25 mm long) and a 2.4 mm tungsten sticking out 5 mm, pointing along -x. The filler rod is a bare 3.2 mm mild-steel TIG rod (drawn yellow in the simulation so the cameras can see it; only the grip sleeve is coloured), leaving the underside of a 25 mm blue nylon grip sleeve (white band) sloping 20 degrees down, its tip 21.25 cm from the sleeve's centre along the rod (32 g in all); the sleeve sits on a steel post at (12, -25) cm, the rod along +x, its tip on a 3 mm black rubber pad. Positions are from the arm bases' midpoint in x and the table's centre line in y, with +y toward the left arm. The screenshot shows the start. Real trial, fixed settings (full list, checks and safety in the README): a DC TIG inverter, electrode negative, high-frequency start, 120 A (confirmed by a test bead; at most 150 A); 2.4 mm 2% lanthanated tungsten; argon 99.99% at 9 L/min, 0.5 s pre-flow, 10 s post-flow; torch cable and hose on an overhead balancer; a bare ER70S-6 rod wiped with acetone, longer than the simulated one (tip 320 mm from the sleeve's centre), since a full bead melts about 150-200 mm and the rod hand moves toward the pool as it shortens; plates ground bright 15 mm each side of the joint and degreased; the fixture table on insulating pads, the work clamp on it; ticks scribed on the outer plate every 5 mm, 12 mm from the joint line. The supervisor, outside the curtains, holds a hold-to-run arc switch, closing it only with the tungsten within 10 mm above the start mark and releasing it at the end mark or to stop; one emergency stop beside it cuts the robots' power and the inverter's output. Welding curtains (EN ISO 25980) close the cell, nobody inside; shade 5-8 filters cover the camera lenses; a fume arm draws from 20-30 cm beside the joint; aluminised sleeves on grippers and forearms; a heat mat round the fixture table; a fire extinguisher.
scoring: Real trial, read once the plates are under 50 C, still clamped (how each reading is made: README). The 200 mm joint is 40 segments of 5 mm between the scribed ticks. A segment is sound when, over its whole 5 mm: the bead's near edge is 9.5 mm or less from the tick line and its far edge 14.5 mm or more (the groove's edges are at 10 and 14 mm), with no sharp bevel corner left at either edge under a 10x loupe; the bead is nowhere below either plate's surface and nowhere more than 3 mm above it; a 0.3 mm feeler gauge enters under neither bead edge (no overlap); and there is no hole through the plate (burn-through; the underside is checked only for holes), no visible crack, no surface pore over 1 mm across, no undercut deeper than 0.5 mm and no arc strike (a melted spot off the bead fails the nearest segment). A defect touching a segment fails it. A rod fused to the plate is left as it is: its segment fails and the rod is not on its rest. Contamination: grey or silver metal on the tungsten's point, or the point blunted, under the loupe after the trial. 0 if the torch or the rod falls off the table, and 0 with no bead. Otherwise 0.9 x the fraction of the 40 segments that are sound (rounded to 0.001), capped at 0.5 after contamination or any burn-through. 1.0 with all 40 sound, no contamination or burn-through, both tools back on their rests (each grip centre within 12 mm in plan and 6 mm in height of its rest position, tilted under 10 degrees, turned under 20 degrees), both hands 6 cm or more from every part of both tools, and tools and hands still for the last 1 s. Simulation (stand-ins; full rules in the README): the arc is on while the held torch's tungsten tip is 2-5 mm above the plates and within 4 mm of the joint line; each segment within 8 mm of it gains that arc time and is molten from 0.5 s. A dab is the rod, in the other hand, lifted 6 mm or more and brought down with the centre of its tip's end within 2.5 mm of the plates' top (at the rod's 20 degree slope, its lowest edge within 1 mm), 3-10 mm ahead of the tungsten, onto a molten segment. A segment is sound with a dab and 3 to 9 s of arc; 9 s is burn-through. Contamination (latched, no arc after): the tungsten within 0.5 mm of the plates or of the rod.
reset_notes: Simulation: lay the torch back on its rest posts and the rod's sleeve back on its post with the tip on the pad; the bead is the score's record and is cleared at reset. Real trial, consumed each time: fit two new plates, bevelled, ground and degreased as in the setup, and scribe their ticks; fit a new rod in the sleeve, cut so its tip is 320 mm from the sleeve's centre (a full bead melts about 150-200 mm of it, leaving 100 mm or more between the sleeve and the arc at the end); check the tungsten with the loupe and regrind or replace it after any contamination, keeping 5 mm of stick-out; refill argon as needed. Measure the plates once under 50 C (about 15 minutes), still clamped; move them only with tongs before then.
fidelity: Rigid bodies with real contact for torch, rod, plates and hands; bevels and clamps are drawn only, so a dab reaches no lower than the plate top. Arc, heat and filler are not simulated: the arc is a tungsten height and position condition, heat is arc time per segment, filler is a counted rod dab over a molten segment. The rod (bare steel, drawn yellow; longer in the real trial) doesn't shorten or stick; no pores, cracks or undercut; cameras unfiltered; no current, gas or hose drag.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (recorded with the earlier wording "the yellow filler rod"; on the revised wording Dream-1 refused: "unsafe instruction, refused: Using a hot welding torch presents severe thermal and fire risks"); demo: 1.0
